title: Everyone who climbed with you
hookLine: Marcus, Rumi, Epictetus, Zhuangzi, Julian, Hillel, Kabir, Thoreau, and the people beside you
tomorrow: a poet reaches a summit and opens a book. what's on the page?

lines: THE NIGHT YOU DROVE ME HOME.
cards: A card that says thanks for everything is kind. A card that says thanks for the night you drove me home is the one that ends up on the fridge. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor, knew the difference.
His private notebook, known now as the Meditations, opens with a list. First on it: his grandfather Verus, and what Marcus learned from him, good character and the governing of his temper.

teach.b: Then he keeps going, a whole first book of debts, each with a name and a gift. His mother: generosity, and a simple way of living, far from the habits of the rich.

His teacher Rusticus: to read carefully, not skim. From Apollonius, to be steady, and to accept favors from friends without being either humbled by them or careless of them. And here's one to tell a friend tonight.
Rusticus is also how Marcus met Epictetus's teaching: he shared the discourses from his own collection. The teacher Marcus quotes later in his notebook arrived because a friend handed him a book.
The first book ends with thanks to the gods for good grandparents, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good friends.
That's the practice in Marcus's first book, named plainly: gratitude with names and specifics, written down, so you remember that your character was handed to you by people.
This path has its own list. Marcus and Epictetus. Rumi's reed.
Zhuangzi's trap and fish. Julian of Norwich and her hazelnut. Hillel, on one foot.
Kabir, Thoreau at his pond, Kuoan's herder.
And the people beside you, who climbed too.

how: Stoic readers keep Marcus's first book as a model of gratitude by name; people on this path write or say a short list of whom they owe and for what.

games.q: what does “everyone who climbed with you” mean?
o: a hiking group that meets on weekend mornings
the well-known names you've memorized from books
the people and teachers who helped you up the path

games.q: Marcus's book of debts: tap the pairs.
p: generosity, a simple way of living
ends thanking the gods for good people

s: the Meditations opens with a list of what Marcus learned from people
book one: his grandfather, his mother, his teachers, each with a gift.
Marcus found Epictetus's teaching on his own in a library
his teacher Rusticus shared the discourses from his own collection.
Stoics taught people to stop feeling grateful
the popular picture of cold Stoics. Marcus's first book is gratitude by name.

games.q: your sister's wedding toast so far says 'thanks to everyone who made today possible.' what would Marcus's first book suggest?
o: name a few people, and one specific thing each one gave.
keep it general, so that nobody feels left out.
skip the thanks; toasts should only be about the couple.
games.why: Marcus opened his notebook with names and gifts: Verus, his mother, Rusticus. Stoic gratitude says who, and what.

practice: Say three names out loud, softly, the way Marcus wrote them: a name, then one thing that person gave you. Touch a finger for each one as you say it. Then let the rest of the two minutes be quiet, hands open.

wordCard.voice: Everyone who climbed with you: Marcus's book of debts, and the long list of names on this path, yours included.

orig.note: Greek: to himself, the Greek title of Marcus's Meditations.

carryVoice: Keep this one: we climbed together, and Marcus began with his grandfather's name. See you near the top.

sources.ref: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 1.1 (Verus), 1.3 (his mother), 1.7 (Rusticus and Epictetus's discourses), 1.17 (thanks to the gods)
